title: Fighting Fire with Fire: Prescribed Burns Save Giant Sequoias from Extreme Wildfires
summary: Giant sequoias, among Earth's most massive and ancient organisms, evolved with frequent low-intensity fires. But after the 2020 Castle Fire and 2021 KNP Complex Fire killed thousands of these titans, their fireproof reputation crumbled. Now, a study published in Nature Communications reveals that prescribed burns—intentional, controlled fires—can dramatically improve their odds. Researchers from UC Davis, USGS, and Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks used airborne lidar and high-resolution satellite imagery to assess fuel conditions and survival for roughly 26,400 sequoias in 19 groves. They found that trees in areas treated with prescribed fire within the previous decade were nearly four times more likely to survive than untreated trees. "Prescribed burns are effective at reducing giant sequoia mortality, even for today's extreme wildfires," said lead author Dan Dixon. Computer models suggest these burns prevented about 1,900 deaths, and if all groves had been treated, an additional 3,900 trees might have survived. The parks have run one of the nation's most extensive prescribed fire programs since the 1960s, creating a natural experiment. Untreated areas accumulated over a century of fuel—dead wood and dense shrubs—that fed catastrophic flames. In contrast, treated groves had less fuel, so fires burned cooler and lower, sparing the sequoias' thick-barked trunks and elevated canopies. Co-author Yufang Jin noted the study's timely relevance as climate change intensifies wildfires. The findings provide robust evidence that proactive fuel reduction isn't just theoretical—it's a lifeline for these irreplaceable giants. As Dixon put it, "If the goal is protecting giant sequoias, prescribed fire is an essential tool."
why_it_matters: As climate change makes wildfires more extreme, learning to coexist with fire through proactive burns will decide whether future generations inherit ancient forests or only photographs of them—a challenge that directly affects the planet's biodiversity and air quality.

background_read: Giant sequoias need fire to reproduce: their cones release seeds when heated, and flames clear competing plants. For thousands of years, lightning-sparked fires and intentional burns by Native American tribes maintained open, low-fuel groves. However, after the 1910 wildfire season, the U.S. government adopted a policy of aggressive fire suppression, causing dead wood to pile up and forests to become dangerously dense.

The Castle Fire (2020) and KNP Complex Fire (2021) were so intense they killed sequoias that had survived centuries of blazes. In response, researchers from UC Davis (a public research university in California's Central Valley), USGS (the U.S. Geological Survey, a scientific agency that studies landscapes and ecosystems), and the National Park Service joined forces to study why some trees lived.

Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks have operated a prescribed fire program since the 1960s—one of the longest-running in the nation. This created a natural experiment: some groves had been treated with low-intensity burns, others had not. That contrast allowed scientists to measure exactly how much protection proactive burning provides, even against modern megafires.

Using airborne lidar, which can pierce through forest canopy to map ground fuel, and satellite images, the team calculated that treated areas had about 75% lower mortality. The study's message has reached policymakers at a time when wildfire seasons are getting longer and more severe due to climate change, and prescribed burning is often limited by air-quality concerns and public fear.

perspectives.description: Prescribed burns offer a proven, cost-effective way to protect irreplaceable ecosystems. The study gives land managers the hard data they need to expand these programs, potentially saving thousands of giant sequoias and many other fire-adapted species. For local communities, it means healthier forests that are less likely to explode into uncontrollable infernos.

Despite the evidence, prescribed burning remains controversial. Smoke from intentional burns can worsen air quality and trigger health problems for nearby residents. There are also risks of burns escaping control—although rare—which fuels public opposition. Some argue that in an era of megadroughts, even treated areas might not survive the most extreme 'firestorm' conditions.

The study is a real-world validation of fire ecology: fire suppression created a fuel backlog, and now returning low-intensity fire acts like a reset button. Historically, many societies have used controlled burns, and this research brings a long-standing indigenous practice into modern science. The pattern is clear—removing fire from a fire-dependent landscape is itself a disturbance.

Scaling up prescribed burns requires training more fire practitioners, adjusting air-quality regulations, and securing funding. New technologies, such as drones for ignition and monitoring, could make burns safer and cheaper. The study may also influence the rewilding movement, as conservationists push to reintroduce fire as a natural process in other fire-adapted forests around the world.
